title: Entry Point & Monorepo Map
description: Start where the binary starts: packages/opencode/src/index.ts is a strict yargs CLI wiring 24 subcommands (run, serve, tui, acp, mcp, models, upgrade, ...) plus logging setup, a one-time JSON-to-SQLite migration with a progress bar, and centralized fatal error formatting. The root README.md gives the front-page story — an open source AI coding agent installable via curl/npm/brew/nix with a desktop beta — and the root package.json defines the Bun workspace monorepo (packages/*, packages/sdk/js) that every later step lives in. Keep this map in mind: the tour descends from this entry into the session core, moves out to the clients, and ends at release.
languageLesson: Bun workspaces: the root package.json's `workspaces` globs let packages import each other via `workspace:*`, while `catalog:` offloads dependency versions to a central table in bun.lock — bump once, upgrade everywhere.

title: CLI Run Modes
description: `opencode run` (cli/cmd/run.ts) is the command most users type first, with three modes: non-interactive single-prompt streaming to stdout, interactive local mode booting the split-footer direct UI with an in-process server, and attach mode against an already-running server. It also handles slash-command execution, JSON event output, and session continue/fork. Notice that command handlers flow through cli/effect-cmd.ts (fan-in 25): like everything in this codebase, the CLI is built on Effect services rather than bare promises.
languageLesson: effectCmd adapts yargs handlers to Effect: each handler returns `Effect<void, CliError, ...>`, so CLI subcommands participate in structured concurrency and typed error handling instead of raw async functions.

title: Config & Instance State
description: Every subcommand eventually loads configuration through config/config.ts — the full opencode.json schema (agents, providers, MCP, LSP, compaction, permissions, plugins) deep-merged across global, project, remote well-known, account/org, and MDM sources with variable substitution. Beneath it sits effect/instance-state.ts, the most-imported file in the package (fan-in 63): a per-directory ScopedCache that lazily initializes state for each project instance and invalidates it on dispose, backing instance-scoped services like Env, File, and Format. These two files establish the pattern you will see everywhere: schema-defined state plus Effect layers scoped to a project directory.
languageLesson: Effect's ScopedCache gives InstanceState its power: per-directory lazy initialization with automatic invalidation on dispose — a scoped service registry rather than a global singleton map.

title: Sessions, Events & Persistence
description: The data backbone: session/session.ts is the core Session service (create/fork/get/list plus message and part updates) whose writes flow through SyncEvent projections rather than direct SQL, while bus/index.ts (fan-in 47) is the typed PubSub event bus fanning those events out to every subscriber. storage/db.ts provides a lazy singleton SQLite client — WAL and busy_timeout pragmas, bundled Drizzle migrations — and session/session.sql.ts defines the schema: session, message, part, todo, session_message, and permission tables with cascading foreign keys. message-v2.ts then hydrates those rows back into messages and converts history into AI SDK model messages for the loop you will meet next.
languageLesson: Drizzle convention in this repo: snake_case property names (e.g. `created_at`) so column names never need string overrides, and WAL mode on SQLite so streaming writes do not block concurrent readers.

title: The Agent Loop
description: The heart of the product: session/prompt.ts is the SessionPrompt service wiring twenty-plus Effect services into the agent run loop, and session/loop/run-loop.ts is that loop — each step filters compacted history, dispatches subtask and compaction parts, triggers auto-compaction on overflow, resolves tools, assembles the system prompt suffix, streams the assistant turn, and exits when the assistant finishes without pending tool calls. session/llm.ts wraps the AI SDK's streamText, merging model and agent options and wiring plugin transform hooks around every request. Read run-loop.ts top to bottom: it is the single best file for understanding what an AI coding agent actually does each turn.
languageLesson: The loop is an `Effect.fn` generator running in an Effect fiber: aborting a prompt propagates structured cancellation through the in-flight LLM stream and any nested tool executions — no manual cleanup chains.

title: System Prompt & Agents
description: Who is the agent? system.ts assembles the system prompt: a cacheable prefix joining the shared core.txt with a provider-specific delta chosen by matchDelta's model-ID regex cascade, plus dynamic <environment> and <skills> sections with semantic skill auto-match. agent.ts is the agent registry defining the built-ins (build, plan, general, explore, scout, compaction, title, summary) with layered permission rulesets, merged with user config overrides per instance. These definitions are exactly what Step 5's loop consults on every turn.
languageLesson: Prompt caching economics: the system prompt is split into a stable prefix (core.txt + provider delta) and a dynamic suffix (environment, skills). Keeping the prefix byte-identical across turns lets providers serve it from KV cache instead of re-billing those tokens.

title: Tool Framework
description: Tools are how the loop touches the world. tool/tool.ts defines Tool.define, the framework every tool passes through — schema decoding of arguments, friendly validation errors, automatic output truncation, and OpenTelemetry spans. registry.ts assembles all built-ins plus plugin tools and filters them per model (e.g. apply_patch instead of edit/write for GPT models), while shell.ts and edit.ts show two representative implementations: tree-sitter-parsed command execution, and exact-or-fuzzy file replacement with per-file locking, BOM handling, and LSP diagnostics.
languageLesson: `Tool.define` is a decorator in functional clothing: it takes a tool's execute and returns a wrapped version with decoding, truncation, and telemetry — every built-in tool inherits this behavior without repeating it.

title: Permissions & Subagents
description: Every risky tool call passes through permission/index.ts: ask() evaluates config rules against DB-persisted approvals with deny always winning, waits on a Deferred with a 5-minute timeout, and reply() resolves prompts and transactionally persists 'always allow' rules. tool/task.ts is the subagent spawner — it enforces permission inheritance and nesting limits, applies subagent tool restrictions, and bridges Effect cancellation to abort the child prompt. Together these files form the security boundary between the model's intent and your filesystem.
languageLesson: Permission evaluation flattens all rule sets then uses `findLast` — last match wins. Ordering matters: config deny is checked first, then persisted 'always allow' approvals, then config allow.

title: Provider Layer
description: The provider layer decouples the agent from any single LLM vendor. provider/provider.ts (fan-in 43) merges the models.dev catalog, config, auth, and plugin contributions into the model list and resolves per-provider AI SDK instances with custom fetch and SSE chunk-watchdog wrapping, handling quirks like Azure regions and Bedrock cross-region routing. transform.ts normalizes opencode's internal message contract to each provider via per-provider transform modules, and models.ts caches the models.dev registry with Flock locking and a build-time snapshot fallback. Step 5's llm.ts is the only consumer that needs to care which vendor is behind a model.
languageLesson: The transform layer is the Adapter pattern at message level: one internal message contract, per-provider modules (anthropic, bedrock, mistral, deepseek, ...) that sanitize and reshape it, so the loop never branches on provider IDs.

title: HTTP API Server
description: `opencode serve` exposes the whole agent over HTTP: server/server.ts builds the Effect layer graph, starts the listener with graceful shutdown and optional mDNS discovery, and serves the web handler app plus the public OpenAPI document. The endpoint surface is assembled in httpapi/api.ts (composition root of root, control, global, and instance-scoped route groups) and httpapi/server.ts — the highest fan-out file in the repo at 73 — which wires roughly forty service layers plus auth, CORS, compression, and workspace-routing middleware. This SSE stream plus REST contract is what the TUI, web app, and SDK in the next steps all speak.
languageLesson: Effect HttpApi is schema-first: request and response types are declared as Effect Schemas and compiled into both runtime validators and the OpenAPI document — the same definitions Step 13's SDK generator consumes.

title: Terminal UI Client
description: The flagship client is the OpenTUI terminal app: tui/app.tsx is the root, bootstrapping the renderer, keymap, stderr capture, and the full command palette (session, model, agent, theme, system toggles) with dialogs and the self-upgrade flow. routes/session/index.tsx (fan-out 66) is the complete conversation screen — user and assistant message renderers, per-tool part views, permission and question prompts, and commands like share, rename, fork, compact, and undo/redo. It talks to the Step 10 HTTP API or runs in-process, which is why every interface stays consistent across clients.
languageLesson: OpenTUI renders TSX to the terminal: elements like `<spinner>` and `<markdown>` are custom renderables, and the component tree diffs like a virtual DOM — the session view is effectively a component over the SSE event stream.

title: Web App & Shared UI
description: packages/app is the SolidJS web client: app.tsx composes the full provider stack (query client, i18n, dialogs, SDK, sync, theming, routing), lazy-loads route pages, and gates rendering on a server health check with a connection-error fallback. pages/session.tsx renders the session view — a bounded history window that reveals cached turns on upward scroll, review/diff tabs, a terminal panel, and the composer region. It is built on packages/ui, the shared component library that also serves the desktop app: default-themes.ts ships 38 built-in themes and i18n/en.ts is the English dictionary every other locale falls back to.
languageLesson: SolidJS fine-grained reactivity: use `createResource` (not `createMemo`) when items can be async — this repo documents a regression where swapping in a memo made list dialogs render empty despite 200 OK API calls.

title: Generated TypeScript SDK
description: All clients converge on @opencode-ai/sdk: the root index re-exports the v2 surface and provides createOpencode(), which boots a local server and returns a connected client pair. v2/client.ts wraps the generated hey-api fetch client with a no-timeout fetch, directory and workspace header injection, an HTML-response guard against version-mismatched servers, and structured error wrapping. Crucially, src/v2/gen is generated code — script/build.ts regenerates openapi.json into TypeScript types and the fetch client, then patches the output, so the Step 10 API schema remains the single source of truth.
languageLesson: Never hand-edit generated code: src/v2/gen is rebuilt by script/build.ts from openapi.json via @hey-api/openapi-ts, with a patch step applied after generation. Server schema changes flow one way — regenerate, then adapt consumers.

title: Docs & Release Pipeline
description: The tour ends with how it ships. packages/web is the Astro/Starlight docs and session-share site — content.config.ts registers the docs collections with locale-checked schemas, and rules.mdx is a representative page explaining AGENTS.md rules and precedence. Release runs through .github/workflows/publish.yml (version computation, cross-built binaries, Windows code-signing, npm/GHCR/AUR publishing) gated upstream by ci.yml's typecheck, while packages/opencode/Dockerfile packages the compiled CLI into a minimal multi-stage Alpine image. From entry point to release, you have now traced the full lifecycle of a change in this monorepo.
languageLesson: Multi-stage Docker with arch selection: both musl binary stages (x64-baseline, arm64) are declared and buildx's TARGETARCH picks one at build time; the runtime stage stays minimal — libgcc, libstdc++, ripgrep — keeping the image small.
